narrative:
The model determined that you have an 80% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process heavily weighs this predicted outcome, your law school application was rejected.

The three factors that most strongly influenced this decision were your academic performance in your third year of law school, your LSAT score, and your first-year academic performance. All three pushed the prediction strongly toward failure rather than success.

Your third-year class ranking placed you in the bottom decile, far below the average ranking of accepted students. This was the single most important reason the model saw a high risk of bar exam failure. Your LSAT score of 19.3 was also substantially lower than the average of 37 for accepted applicants, providing the second-largest push toward a negative outcome. Finally, your first-year ranking in the lowest decile, compared to an average around the sixth decile for successful applicants, added further weight to the prediction of failure.

Although your undergraduate GPA of 3.20 is nearly identical to the average of accepted students and your plan to attend full-time is the most common choice among those admitted, these factors were not enough to offset the concerns raised by your law school grades and LSAT performance.

You should focus on improving your substantive legal knowledge and test-taking skills before retaking the bar exam. Consider structured bar preparation courses, additional coursework, or mentorship programs that have helped students with similar profiles succeed on a second attempt. Once you have passed the bar, many law schools will reconsider your application.
